subject: Browser-facing freshness and live UI update design

cases.scenario: A live operations dashboard shows status counts that change every few seconds. The browser only needs server-to-browser updates and can refetch summaries by ID or version.
cases.context: The team asks whether to use polling, SSE, or WebSocket.
cases.question: How should the agent choose the transport and browser state contract?
expected_flags: Starts with the freshness contract: acceptable age, disruption rules, and recovery behavior.
Prefers SSE or adaptive polling over WebSocket because updates are one-way.
Uses small invalidation/version messages rather than treating push as full truth by default.
Refetches or reconciles authoritative server state after update signals.
Shows timestamp, connection state, or stale indicator.
expected_fix_hints: Use WebSocket only if the browser must send frequent low-latency messages on the same channel.
Verify hosting, proxy, browser, and runtime connection limits.
Centralize the subscription or query-cache invalidation path.
absent_signals: Do not choose WebSocket only because the feature is called real-time.
Do not hide freshness or connection status.
Do not make every widget open its own live channel.

Surfaces this expected flag: Refetches or reconciles authoritative server state after update signals.
Surfaces this expected flag: Shows timestamp, connection state, or stale indicator.

Recommends this expected fix or action: Verify hosting, proxy, browser, and runtime connection limits.

cases.scenario: A browser loses an EventSource connection during a deploy. It reconnects automatically, but updates may have occurred while the connection was down.
cases.context: A developer argues that built-in reconnect means the view is current.
cases.question: How should the agent respond?
expected_flags: Says built-in reconnect is not enough to certify the view is current.
Requires last seen event ID, version, cursor, timestamp, or equivalent marker.
Requires catch-up fetch or full refetch before clearing stale status.
Shows reconnecting/stale status until authoritative state is reconciled.
Deduplicates updates that arrive through both catch-up and the live channel.
expected_fix_hints: Persist or track the last applied version in the browser/cache.
Design server support for catch-up by ID/version/timestamp where needed.
If missed events cannot be determined, perform a full refetch.
absent_signals: Do not assume EventSource reconnect replays every missed event.
Do not keep a Live badge during unknown freshness.
Do not clear stale state before reconciliation.

cases.scenario: A table auto-refreshes as new rows arrive. While a user is editing filters and selecting rows, the table reorders and clears selection.
cases.context: The product still needs to communicate that new data exists.
cases.question: How should the agent repair the interaction?
expected_flags: Identifies silent auto-refresh during active work as disruptive.
Uses a new-data banner or user-controlled refresh when updates would reorder or clear context.
Preserves selection, scroll, filters, and input state when auto-apply is safe.
Keeps freshness visible with timestamps, badges, or update counts.
Defines when auto-refresh is safe versus user-mediated.
expected_fix_hints: Apply automatically only to low-disruption counters or append-only areas where position is preserved.
Separate freshness signaling from applying the update.
Verify with interaction-feedback for generic pending/error feedback if needed.
absent_signals: Do not silently replace an active interactive view.
Do not hide that new data is waiting.
Do not treat this as a low-level stream protocol problem.

cases.scenario: A user marks a notification as read in a live notification panel. The action should feel instant, but the server can reject it and other live updates may arrive at the same time.
cases.context: The team asks how to make the UI feel immediate without lying.
cases.question: What pattern should the agent apply?
expected_flags: Allows optimistic UI because the action is reversible and low risk.
Shows pending state and keeps previous state for rollback.
Reconciles with authoritative server state after success or failure.
Handles concurrent live updates without overwriting newer server state.
Shows failure feedback and recovery.
expected_fix_hints: Use a mutation/update mechanism that can roll back or invalidate the cache.
Treat optimistic state as provisional until confirmed.
Route generic feedback details to interaction-feedback if the task is not freshness-specific.
absent_signals: Do not present speculative state as final.
Do not use optimistic updates for irreversible or high-stakes actions.

cases.scenario: An API emits thousands of chunks over HTTP and the user asks how to model producer, stream, consumer, backpressure, framing, and termination.
cases.context: The task is about stream protocol semantics, not browser view freshness.
cases.question: Should real-time-updates own this request?
expected_flags: This is streaming-architecture.
Low-level producer/consumer/backpressure/termination semantics are out of scope.
real-time-updates may compose only if a browser view later needs freshness UX on top.
expected_fix_hints: Route stream protocol design to streaming-architecture.
Return to real-time-updates for dashboard stale state, reconnect status, or transport UX decisions.
absent_signals: Do not design backpressure inside this skill.
Do not confuse SSE transport semantics with browser freshness UX.

cases.scenario: A team asks for topic names, event envelope fields, schema versions, replay rules, and compatibility rules for outbound events.
cases.context: No browser freshness behavior has been requested.
cases.question: Should real-time-updates own this request?
expected_flags: This is event-contract-design.
Event envelope, topic naming, compatibility, and replay are out of scope for browser freshness.
real-time-updates may later consume event notifications as invalidation signals.
expected_fix_hints: Route async event contract design to event-contract-design.
Use real-time-updates only for how a browser learns and reconciles after the event affects state.
absent_signals: Do not define the event schema in this skill.
Do not treat browser push as the event-contract owner.

cases.scenario: A slow export needs to move out of a request handler. The user asks for queue state, retry policy, cancellation, checkpointing, and worker concurrency.
cases.context: The browser may later show progress, but the current task is durable execution design.
cases.question: Should real-time-updates own this request?
expected_flags: This is background-jobs.
Durable execution, retries, cancellation, checkpoints, and worker concurrency are out of scope.
real-time-updates owns how the browser learns about the durable progress state after it exists.
expected_fix_hints: Use real-time-updates for polling/SSE/WebSocket progress visibility and stale status.
absent_signals: Do not design worker execution under this skill.
Do not skip durable progress state and rely only on a live connection.
